By late 1948, most of the Soviet Union — the black area on this map — was legally off-limits to every foreigner on Earth. Diplomats, journalists, tourists: didn't matter. You needed permission just to travel by train.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ On Sept 30, 1948, Moscow issued a new list of closed areas, followed on Oct 27 by rules requiring foreigners to travel through them only by public transport, with permission needed to go more than 50km off the route.

2/ A 25km-wide closed strip ran along the entire Soviet land border with non-Communist states, sealing the frontier from view. Foreigners caught wandering off the approved route risked arrest as suspected spies.

3/ One closed strip stretched 50km on either side of the railway from Zheleznodorozhnyy to Vorkuta — a line built by Gulag prisoners to reach Vorkuta's coal mines, one of the deadliest forced-labor complexes in the USSR.

4/ The US State Department called the restrictions "unprecedented in the history of any nation in time of peace." Western diplomats posted in Moscow suddenly couldn't legally drive to most of the country they lived in.

5/ The same years produced an even stranger category: closed cities that officially didn't exist. Arzamas-16, founded in 1946 to build the Soviet atomic bomb, was missing from maps entirely — no name, no dot, nothing.

6/ Some outlasted the USSR itself. Russia still maintains dozens of "closed administrative-territorial formations" today — mostly nuclear and military sites outsiders cannot enter without a permit.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
